rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.5 and 3.1-3.3, Tables 5-7, Figs 3-5 <U+2014> the authors report their own canal inflow records, bi-weekly piezometer measurements (2010-2013), SWAP model runs per land use, a calibrated/validated percolation-groundwater depth relationship, and scenario simulations for the San Giorgio East district.
rows.notes: The study does not test drip irrigation. It analyses a scenario of replacing continuous submergence of rice with flush irrigation (intermittent surface irrigation of rice grown as an upland crop, 150 mm applications on demand) in a ~500 ha district of Northern Italy. Its own result is that the district-wide shift to flush irrigation reduces percolation (recharge) from ~3200 mm to ~1100-1400 mm, deepens summer groundwater by ~35 cm, makes the 15-day maize rotation inadequate and raises maize irrigation requirement by ~50% (750 to 1050 mm, FA-10 scenario, Table 7); rice irrigation reduction falls from ~80% (no feedback) to ~60% (feedback). The mechanism of reduced recharge raising demand of other crops is thus shown, but for flush irrigation, not drip, so Q2 is 'no' with technology_mismatch. Additionally the scenario outputs (groundwater depth under FI, maize demand) are model projections not compared with measurements of the real system under the new regime; only the present-state percolation-groundwater relationship was validated (R2 0.90, NS 0.82 for 2013). Authors do state limitations (empirical relation valid only within calibrated range; results specific to highly permeable soils; yield gaps and ecosystem services not addressed) and standard deviations across years (Tables 5-8), but these are not credited because Q2 is 'no'.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a district-scale scenario modelling analysis of flush (intermittent surface) irrigation of rice versus continuous submergence; drip irrigation is not studied or mentioned.
